Issued at 226 PM CDT Wed Jul 29 2026

Main concern in the forecast is the ongoing smoke, both at the 
surface and aloft, and the return of shower and thunderstorms 
(potentially severe) with beneficial rain in the forecast across the 
region late tonight through Thursday night. As of 2pm, temperatures 
are in the upper 80s to around 100 with dewpoints in the upper 60s 
to the upper 70s, highest James River and eastward thanks in part to 
peak evapotranspiration and south to southeast winds. Heat indices 
range in the 90s to the lower 100s. Went ahead and expanded the Heat 
Advisory to cover the remaining forecast area with the exception of 
Codington and Hamlin. Besides fair weather cumulus over central SD 
and portions of NESD skies remain free of clouds with ongoing smoke 
and hazy skies. Smoke from the wildfires out west will continue to 
affect the region with lighter concentrations of near surface smoke 
continuing through the rest of the evening and tonight before 
lifting northward Thursday morning for a few hours before moving 
back in mainly east of the Mo River late Thursday night/Friday 
morning. This may continue to bring a reduction in visibility and 
affect people who are sensitive to smoke. Periods of smoke 
aloft/haze will continue through at least the end of the week.

The Northern Plains continues to be under the upper level ridge with 
its mid level high over the southern CONUS and winds across the CWA 
slightly west to to northwest flow. A shortwave (which originated 
over Arizona) will continue to track northeastward and over Wyoming 
by 00Z Thursday with a lee north to south oriented surface trough 
along the western Dakotas and eastern WY/MT. The CWA will be within 
the warm sector (between this and a high over MN) with ongoing south 
to southeasterly winds at the surface to 850mb and ongoing moist 
air. By 06Z, there really only seems to be a slight shift eastward 
in the surface trough which is connecting to a low over the Northern 
Rockies. By this time, the majority of the CAMs keep any convection 
just to the west of the CWA. Between 12-18Z the center of the low on 
this surface trough really only shifts a bit east and over south 
central SD. Widely scattered showers and thunderstorms will mainly 
continue along and west of the Missouri River. However, NBM is a bit 
more bullish and has pops extending to the James River. Through the 
afternoon and evening the surface trough will orient itself more 
northeast to southwest over the eastern half of SD/NE with the 
convection continuing to track eastward with additional development 
of shower and thunderstorms across the entire CWA. CAMS do vary 
quite a bit on timing and the location of development/storm track 
through the midday Thursday. So low confidence remains, however, NBM 
does a good job keeping the pops widespread due to this. Later on in 
the afternoon a few of a models do show the potential of storms 
clustering and eventually growing upscale/cold pool development and 
forming into a line of storms extending from Nebraska through 
central and northeastern SD into MN where it will track 
east/southeast and hopefully out of the eastern CWA by late Thursday 
night. HRRR indicates the potential for a bowing segments, however, 
as of now this looks to be south and east of our CWA.

Looking at the mesoscale parameters, the low level moisture will be 
abundant, as mentioned, as dewpoints will overall be in be in the 
the upper 60s to the upper 70s through Friday evening. SB/MUCape 
will generally be around 1000j/kg or less this evening and overnight 
with values increasing by midday Thursday, ranging from 1000-2500 
j/kg highest over northeastern SD. However, 21Z and after values 
decrease to around 1000-1500 j/kg and diminishing even more after 
sunset. However, RAP is much higher with CAPE values of 2000 to 3000 
j/kg with some areas indicating 4K! This looks to be a high CAPE low 
shear setup as bulk shear looks to remain below 30kts and no real 
LLJ. RAP soundings indicate low level lapse rates will be steeper 
whereas mid level lapse rates are not as steep with DCAPE values 
above 1000 j/kg early Thursday morning but does decrease below 
1000j/kg by the afternoon. So the main threat with the storms will 
be damaging wind gusts of 60 to potentially 70 mph with a few storms 
possibly producing quarter size hail. If the line of storms does 
form/grow upscale and/or potentially bow over any part of the CWA 
then wind gusts could potentially be higher. Main caveat will be the 
cloud cover which could keep instability on the lower side for 
Thursday as well as a cap over much of the region setting up late 
tonight through the morning before breaking Thursday afternoon. A 
Marginal Risk (1/5) continues over north central SD for the 
convection overnight/early Thursday. A Slight Risk (2/5) for 
portions of south central SD with a Marginal Risk covering the rest 
of the CWA for Thursday with the main threat being damaging wind
